item.title: RBI urges banks to expedite MSME lending, reduce reliance on collateral
item.description: The central bank has called for greater use of digital lending channels, expansion of receivables financing, and early identification and resolution of stress among MSME borrowers ...
item.dc:creator: Aathira Varier
item.content:encoded: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has urged banks to expedite credit sanctions to micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and reduce their reliance on collateral, encouraging cash-flow-based lending through digital channels to improve access to finance for the sector. At the 31st meeting of the Standing Advisory Committee (SAC) on MSME credit in Kolkata, Deputy Governor Swaminathan J called for greater use of the Unified Lending Interface (ULI) and other digital channels to facilitate lending to MSMEs, the RBI said in a press release. He also emphasised the need to expand the use of the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) for receivables financing and strengthen early identification and resolution of stress among MSME borrowers. The meeting reviewed the flow of working capital and investment credit to MSMEs, lending to first-time borrowers, and credit guarantee coverage. Discussions also covered the enhanced limit for collateral-free lending to micro and small enterprises, settlement of invoices of central public sector enterprises (CPSEs) through TReDS, and key provisions of the MSMED (Amendment) Act, 2026. Recognising the contribution of MSMEs to India's economic growth and development goals, the deputy governor also called on industry associations to actively participate in the RBI's outreach initiatives, including town halls and district-level MSME SAMVAAD meetings. Such engagements would help improve awareness of credit-related initiatives and enable industry associations to raise concerns of their members with banks, according to the RBI. The meeting was attended by representatives of the Ministry of MSME, the Department of Financial Services, select banks, Sidbi, Nabard, CGTMSE, NCGTC, KVIC, the Indian Banks' Association, and national, regional, and state-level MSME associations.

item.title: X rolls out parental controls for teens, but parents face a limitation
item.description: The new features allow parents to set screen-time limits, approve followers and restrict direct messages, but teenagers must consent to supervision and can retain access to their private chats ...
item.dc:creator: Apexa Rai
item.content:encoded: Social media platform X has introduced parental controls for teenage accounts, allowing parents and guardians to monitor screen time, approve new followers and restrict content recommendations. However, the new features come with a limitation that teenagers must agree to link their accounts with those of their parents before supervision can begin. The announcement, made by X's official Safety account, marks the platform's introduction of dedicated parental supervision tools. The features are designed for users aged 13 to 17 and give parents some control over their children's activity without granting them access to private conversations or browsing histories.How will X's parental controls work?Parents and guardians can link their accounts with those of their teenagers through an invitation. The teenager must accept the request before the parental controls can be activated. The invitation remains valid for 72 hours. Once the accounts are linked, parents can view how much time their teenager has spent on X over the previous seven days and set daily screen-time limits. They can also restrict access to certain features and manage aspects of their children's interactions on the platform. X allows parents to require approval before new accounts can follow their teenagers. Enabling this option also makes the teenager's account private. Parents can additionally restrict recommendations and videos in the For You feed to accounts their teenagers already follow. They can filter content by blocking specific words and switch off the display of sensitive media. ALSO READ: WhatsApp partners with Jio, Verizon, more to bring travel eSIM data plansParents can restrict DMs, but cannot read private messagesThe new controls allow parents to decide who can send direct messages to their teenagers. They can also see which accounts their children have exchanged one-to-one messages with. However, parents will not be able to read the actual conversations. They will also not have access to their teenagers' search or viewing histories, or be able to post on their behalf or take control of their accounts. ALSO READ: Apple removes Chinese AI chatbot from App Store over child safety concernsTeenagers can refuse parental supervisionOne of the key limitations of the new feature is that parents cannot activate supervision without their teenagers' consent. The teenager must accept the invitation sent by the parent before the accounts can be linked. This gives teenagers the option to decline parental supervision, even if their parents want to enable the controls. A parent can supervise up to five teenage accounts, while each teenager can be linked to only one parent or guardian.What happens when teenagers turn 18?The parental supervision arrangement is intended for users aged 13 to 17. The supervision link automatically ends when the teenager turns 18.

Sebi aims to cut FPI onboarding time to five business days: Chairman Pandey said the regulator has also proposed removing the additional disclosure framework for FPIs, bringing India's regulatory framework closer to global standards

Over the past few months, Sebi has taken several measures to ease the compliance burden for FPIs | Image: Bloomberg

Press Trust of India New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Nov 27 2026 | 3:55 PM IST

Listen to This Article

Markets regulator Sebi is aiming to reduce the onboarding time for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) from several months to as little as five business days through digital workflows and system integration, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday. Addressing the 17th Capital Markets Conference organised by ASSOCHAM, Pandey said the regulator has also proposed removing the additional disclosure framework for FPIs, bringing India's regulatory framework closer to global standards. "Through digital workflows and system integration, we aim to cut FPI onboarding from months to as little as five business days," Pandey said. Over the past few months, Sebi has taken several measures to ease the compliance burden for FPIs.

Under the SWAGAT-FI (Single Window Automatic and Generalised Access for Trusted Foreign Investors) initiative, around 740 FPIs, accounting for nearly 17 per cent of FPI assets under custody, have registered. Also Read

"SWAGAT-FI gives trusted, low-risk FPIs single-window access, simpler compliance and longer KYC review cycles," he added. On the regulatory front, Pandey said Sebi is undertaking a comprehensive review of the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) framework to eliminate duplicative disclosures in filings with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA). The regulator also plans to replace multiple stock exchange fines for the same compliance lapse with a single penalty. Sebi is simultaneously reviewing the Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) framework, which governs initial public offerings (IPOs), follow-on public offerings (FPOs), preferential issues and qualified institutional placements (QIPs). The review will also cover the SME IPO framework and the Innovators Growth Platform.

For stock brokers, the regulator is exploring a graded compliance framework under which regulatory obligations would be aligned with a broker's scale, client exposure and dependence on technology. Pandey said the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is also working towards harmonising the regulatory frameworks governing Investment Advisers and Mutual Fund Distributors. On the technology front, the regulator is exploring the development of a domestically governed artificial intelligence (AI) model for the securities market, enabling smaller regulated entities to access secure and affordable AI solutions. Guidelines on the responsible use of AI are being prepared, while a proposed AI sandbox will allow innovators to test applications in a controlled environment, he said.

In the corporate bond market, Sebi is developing a market-making framework in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Ministry of Finance, focusing on liquidity, market infrastructure and access to repo facilities. Fixed Income Channel Partners will help expand bond distribution via regulated online platforms, while Phase II of Demat 2.0 will enable secondary-market trading in tokenised bonds. In the cash market, the regulator is reviewing the framework for short selling and securities lending and borrowing (SLB) to improve liquidity and price discovery. For Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), the regulator is simplifying requirements linked to investor consent, related-party transactions, co-investments and exits.

In the case of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs), Sebi aims to reduce the listing timeline from six working days to three days and simplify the process for rights issues. Highlighting the growth of India's capital markets, Pandey said companies raised around Rs 9 lakh crore through equity and debt in the first seven months of the current financial year. So far, 235 IPOs have collectively raised approximately Rs 1.45 lakh crore, while more than Rs 5 lakh crore has been mobilised through corporate bonds.
